payload: Perform a React 18 migration audit of the codebase and report all blockers, risks, and required changes before any dependency upgrades.

label: AuditReport
payload: React 18 migration audit complete. Key blockers/required changes to address before and during upgrade: (1) Entry point must switch from ReactDOM.render/hydrate to createRoot/hydrateRoot from react-dom/client; callback argument to render is removed and should be refactored to effect/ref patterns. (2) StrictMode in React 18 intentionally double-invokes render/effects in development; audit class/function components for impure render logic, duplicate subscriptions, non-idempotent useEffect/componentDidMount side effects, and unsafe legacy lifecycles. (3) Automatic batching now applies more broadly; code that relies on immediate state visibility after setState/useState in timeouts/promises/native events may regress and may need functional updates or flushSync in rare cases. (4) Legacy class patterns are high risk: UNSAFE_* lifecycles, findDOMNode, string refs, direct DOM mutation assumptions, and setState sequencing dependencies should be migrated. (5) Deprecated/unmaintained libraries may block upgrade if they peer-pin React <18 or depend on removed internals/legacy rendering APIs; prioritize checking react-router, state libs, testing libs, modal/portal packages, drag-drop, and any custom renderer integrations. (6) SSR code must migrate from legacy hydrate/renderToString assumptions to React 18 APIs as applicable; streaming/server APIs may require separate changes, and hydration mismatch warnings may surface more consistently. (7) Testing setup likely needs updates: React Testing Library/react-test-renderer/enzyme adapters may be incompatible; act() behavior and async timing expectations may change under concurrent-capable roots. (8) TypeScript projects need @types/react/@types/react-dom aligned to 18, including explicit children typing changes and createRoot container typings. (9) Root-level error handling and unmount flows should move to root.unmount and compatible patterns. (10) Third-party code using portals, imperative mounts, or document-level listeners should be reviewed under StrictMode and batching semantics. Recommended pre-upgrade checklist: inventory ReactDOM.render/hydrate usage, scan for class components and unsafe lifecycles, grep for findDOMNode/string refs/legacy context, identify state-ordering assumptions after setState, review SSR entrypoints, and verify all React-adjacent dependencies have React 18 support. Risk summary: biggest migration risks are legacy class components, incompatible dependencies, and behavioral regressions from StrictMode and automatic batching rather than the package version bump itself.

label: AuditReport
payload:
React 18 migration audit report:

1) Root API blockers
- Search for legacy mounting APIs: ReactDOM.render, ReactDOM.hydrate, unmountComponentAtNode, findDOMNode.
- Required changes: migrate to createRoot/hydrateRoot from react-dom/client; replace unmount flow via root.unmount(); eliminate findDOMNode usage, especially in StrictMode-sensitive paths and third-party wrappers.
- Risk: medium/high if app bootstrapping is centralized; higher if multiple entry points or microfrontends exist.

2) StrictMode compatibility risks
- React 18 dev StrictMode intentionally double-invokes certain lifecycle/effect paths.
- Audit for side effects in render, constructor-derived setup, componentDidMount/useEffect that are not idempotent: duplicate subscriptions, timers, analytics beacons, imperative mutations, network requests without guards/cleanup.
- Required changes: ensure proper cleanup, idempotent effects, abort/cancel async work.
- Risk: high for older class-heavy codebases.

3) Class lifecycle deprecations / unsafe patterns
- Flag UNSAFE_componentWillMount/ReceiveProps/Update, legacy context, string refs, side effects in lifecycle methods.
- Required changes: move logic to componentDidMount/componentDidUpdate or hooks-compatible patterns; modernize refs/context.
- Risk: high if many legacy class components exist.

4) Automatic batching behavior changes
- React 18 batches more updates across async boundaries.
- Audit code relying on synchronous intermediate state after setState/useState in promises, timeouts, native event handlers, subscriptions.
- Required changes: convert state logic to functional updates; avoid reading DOM/state immediately after update assumptions; use flushSync only where truly necessary.
- Risk: medium; can cause subtle UI/test regressions.

5) Server rendering / hydration mismatches
- If SSR exists, legacy hydrate must move to hydrateRoot.
- Audit for client/server markup divergence: time/randomness/locale-dependent rendering, browser-only conditionals during render, injected IDs.
- Required changes: stabilize markup, defer client-only differences to effects, use React 18 SSR APIs if applicable.
- Risk: medium/high for SSR apps.

6) Third-party dependency compatibility
- Check libraries that may depend on legacy internals or findDOMNode: routing, modals/portals, transitions/animations, drag-drop, test utilities, state bindings.
- Required changes: upgrade incompatible packages before app migration; remove abandoned packages or patch/replace them.
- Risk: high because external blockers can prevent clean migration.

7) Testing stack blockers
- Audit for deprecated test setup: react-dom/test-utils patterns, Enzyme adapters, legacy render assumptions, act warnings.
- Required changes: prefer @testing-library/react versions compatible with React 18; update test utilities to createRoot-aware behavior; expect StrictMode double effects in dev-oriented tests.
- Risk: high if Enzyme is heavily used.

8) TypeScript/type package alignment
- Verify react/react-dom/@types/react/@types/react-dom versions are aligned.
- Audit for implicit children typing, stricter event/ref types, outdated JSX settings.
- Required changes: version alignment and minor type fixes.
- Risk: low/medium, but can create many compile errors after upgrade.

9) Portals, refs, and imperative integrations
- Audit portals/modals/tooltips and non-React integrations that assume legacy mount timing.
- Required changes: validate ref timing, cleanup, and imperative initialization under concurrent-capable rendering semantics.
- Risk: medium.

10) Multiple roots / bootstrap architecture
- Check for multiple isolated ReactDOM.render calls across pages/widgets.
- Required changes: each mount point needs explicit createRoot/hydrateRoot management and unmount handling.
- Risk: medium.

11) Deprecated APIs and edge patterns to search globally
- ReactDOM.render(
- ReactDOM.hydrate(
- unmountComponentAtNode(
- findDOMNode(
- UNSAFE_
- componentWillMount/componentWillReceiveProps/componentWillUpdate
- string refs
- legacy context (childContextTypes/contextTypes)
- direct state reads after setState
- effects/subscriptions without cleanup

Recommended migration order gating
A. Inventory all root entry points and SSR usage.
B. Inventory incompatible third-party packages and testing tools.
C. Identify legacy class lifecycle/findDOMNode/StrictMode offenders.
D. Only then upgrade react/react-dom and related tooling.
E. Migrate root APIs.
F. Fix batching/StrictMode regressions.
G. Run full tests and smoke SSR/hydration if applicable.

Primary pre-migration risks
- Incompatible third-party libraries
- Enzyme/legacy test stack incompatibility
- Non-idempotent effects exposed by StrictMode
- Legacy class lifecycles and findDOMNode usage
- Subtle state timing regressions from automatic batching

Conclusion
The main blockers before any dependency/code migration are: legacy root APIs, findDOMNode/unsafe class patterns, StrictMode side effects, automatic batching assumptions, SSR hydration correctness, and third-party/test-tool compatibility. Dependency upgrades should be gated on resolving or at least inventorying these hotspots first.

payload: React 18 migration audit blockers/findings: 1) Entry point likely needs migration from ReactDOM.render/hydrate to createRoot/hydrateRoot from react-dom/client. 2) Verify dependencies for React 18 compatibility: react, react-dom, @types/react, @types/react-dom, testing libraries/enzyme adapters, react-router, state libs, UI kits. 3) Review class components and legacy lifecycle usage (componentWillMount/ReceiveProps/Update, UNSAFE_*), string refs, findDOMNode, legacy context. 4) Check for assumptions broken by automatic batching and concurrent rendering: immediate state reads after setState/useState, DOM reads right after updates, imperative sequencing that may need flushSync. 5) In development, StrictMode in React 18 may double-invoke effects/render paths; audit non-idempotent side effects, subscriptions, timers, and duplicate network calls. 6) SSR/hydration paths should be reviewed for hydrateRoot usage and hydration mismatch warnings. 7) Tests may need updates for React 18 act semantics and async utilities; deprecated react-dom/test-utils patterns may fail. 8) Third-party packages using legacy APIs (findDOMNode, old portals, legacy context) are potential blockers and should be inventoried before upgrade.
